title: Pull Requests
tagline: A pull request isn't a Git feature at all -- it's GitHub's UI wrapped around a branch and a diff you already understand.

concept.label: What
concept.text: A pull request (PR) proposes merging one branch into another, with GitHub's UI showing the diff, discussion, and review status.

concept.label: Why
concept.text: Direct pushes to main skip review entirely -- PRs are the checkpoint where a second person looks before code lands.

concept.label: How
concept.text: Push a branch to GitHub, open a PR from it, request review, address comments with new commits, then merge.

concept.label: When
concept.text: Any change to a shared/production branch on a team project -- even a solo project benefits from the habit.

concept.label: Where
concept.text: The standard workflow every other chapter's techniques (branching, rebasing, history) feed into.

mnemonic.label: P.R.M.
mnemonic.text: Push (the branch) -> Review (get eyes on it) -> Merge (land it) -- the PR lifecycle

sandboxNote.text: this needs a real GitHub repo -- fork any public repo (or use your own from Module 3) to open a real PR against.

code:
git switch -c add-contributing-guide
echo "# Contributing" > CONTRIBUTING.md
git add CONTRIBUTING.md
git commit -m "Add CONTRIBUTING.md"
git push origin add-contributing-guide   # PUSH: branch now exists on GitHub too

# on github.com: click "Compare & pull request" -- write a clear title +
# description of WHAT changed and WHY, then "Create pull request"

# a reviewer leaves a comment asking for a change -- respond with more commits:
echo "## How to contribute" >> CONTRIBUTING.md
git add CONTRIBUTING.md
git commit -m "Address review feedback"
git push origin add-contributing-guide   # the SAME PR updates automatically

# once approved, on github.com: "Merge pull request" -- MERGE, done

cycle.title: Read the concept table once
cycle.text: The reframe worth internalising: a PR is just a labeled diff between two branches, sitting on a server, that people can comment on. Nothing about it changes what Git itself is doing underneath.

cycle.title: Type the code yourself — no copy-paste
cycle.text: Open a real PR (even against your own repo, even alone) -- push a branch, click through GitHub's PR creation flow yourself, and actually read the diff view it generates.
cycle.hint: If you have no collaborator to review it, open the PR anyway and self-review by reading GitHub's diff view as if you were someone else seeing this code for the first time.

cycle.title: Apply it to your own data
cycle.text: Open a PR, then push a SECOND commit to the same branch after opening it, and confirm on GitHub that the PR updated automatically instead of needing a new one.

cycle.title: Reflect & note
cycle.text: What did GitHub's diff view show you that a plain terminal git diff didn't (or vice versa)?
cycle.placeholder: e.g. GitHub's view let me leave an inline comment on one specific line, right in the diff -- that's the review workflow piece a terminal diff can't replicate on its own...

cycle.title: Tick off before moving on
checklist: I can explain what a PR actually is (a labeled diff, not new Git tech).
I pushed a branch and opened a real PR on GitHub myself.
I pushed a follow-up commit and watched the same PR update.
I read GitHub's diff view closely, as a reviewer would.
I wrote a reflection note above.
